case_study_insert.main_stem: Amberhill Artisan Bakery (AAB) is a private limited company in the artisan bakery sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Leila Haddad, it supplies sourdough, wholegrain loaves and pastries to supermarket chains and independent cafes along the coast, operating a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. AAB plans to invest $620,000 in a central production kitchen with an online pre-order platform, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.40 a unit and a selling price of $8.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. AAB faces rising unsold-stock waste, now 7% of daily output, and absenteeism has climbed to 8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The central bakery produced 24,800 units last quarter at a mis-bake defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.1% a year ago. Unsold-stock waste fell from 11% to 7% of daily output, while customer complaints fell from 26 to 15 per month. A survey of 400 in-store customers found 58% would pre-order via a mobile app and 46% buy sourdough every week. Average delivery time to branch stores is 2.1 days. Off-the-job hygiene certification at the technical college costs $700 per employee; 18 of 38 staff need recertification, while on-the-job coaching on the new convection ovens continues.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Amberhill Artisan Bakery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $11.90 to $12.74 per hour from April 2026, increasing total wage bills. (3) Wheat flour and butter input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, food-price inflation is running at 7.2%, while consumer spending on premium bakery products grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: AAB plans to fund part of its central production kitchen with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AAB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs AAB nothing in interest or repayments, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and services a $400,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid as financing cost can absorb the 9.6% rise in flour and butter input costs, keeping the $8.00 sourdough affordable for supermarket buyers and defending AAB's $3.60 contribution per unit at a time when margins are already being squeezed across the bakery sector.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to the bank loan, so the $620,000 central kitchen and online pre-order platform are not at risk of repossession if pre-order demand from the 58% of surveyed app-users disappoints. It also keeps ownership with Leila Haddad and her family, so no lender can impose conditions on how the kitchen is run or on future price rises, and AAB keeps full flexibility to reinvest profits into further capacity once the online range proves itself.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to AAB's expansion, costs and ownership.

questions.question_text: AAB is launching its online pre-order sourdough range to supermarket customers. Consider print advertising in supermarket magazines, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should AAB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print advertising in supermarket magazines: Supermarket magazine ads appear exactly where AAB's target shoppers decide what to buy and can carry the eco-hygiene story of the new kitchen. However, print has long lead times, declining circulation, limited interactivity and no way to drive immediate pre-orders on the new app, so its cost per pre-order is likely to be high for a business investing $620,000 and producing 100,000 units a year.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is affordable, suits time-sensitive launch messages and reaches the coast-wide catchment where AAB already delivers in 2.1 days. Its reach is limited to one region, however, while AAB supplies supermarket chains beyond that catchment, and radio cannot show the sourdough itself or capture the 58% of surveyed shoppers who said they would pre-order via a mobile app.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family-lifestyle influencers can show AAB's sourdough being baked, sliced and pre-ordered, targeted precisely at the 58% of the 400 surveyed customers willing to use the app and the 46% who buy sourdough weekly. Cost per reached shopper is low, results are measurable in clicks and pre-orders, and national supermarket listings can be supported at scale. Drawbacks are influencer credibility risk, slower compounding reach than broadcast media, and dependence on platform algorithms.

Recommendation: AAB should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact segment identified in its own research, reinforces the pre-order platform, scales nationally and fits a $620,000 investment with a ten-year bank loan. Print advertising is rejected as too slow, too passive and too weak at driving app pre-orders, and local radio is rejected as too narrow for supermarket chains beyond the coast; AAB should add modest in-store tasting sessions in partner supermarkets to support the influencer campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AAB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AAB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print advertising and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: AAB's absenteeism has reached 8% and unsold-stock waste is still high. Explain two benefits for AAB of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its bakery teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives AAB's 38 staff a genuine voice in rota planning, bake schedules and waste reduction, which satisfies esteem and social needs on Maslow's hierarchy and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help decide oven loading and delivery timetables are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the 8% absenteeism rate and reducing the disruption it causes to the 2.1-day branch delivery promise and the 100,000-unit output plan.

Point 2: Involving the bakers in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who handle dough and convection ovens daily, improving first-time bake quality and pushing the 2.6% mis-bake defect rate down further. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving the $700 per employee off-the-job hygiene recertification cost at the technical college and protecting consistency for the 400 surveyed customers, 46% of whom buy sourdough weekly and expect reliable availability. Used together, these benefits give AAB the attendance reliability and the quality ownership it needs to hold the 100,000-unit plan while absenteeism sits at 8% and branch delivery stays at 2.1 days.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to AAB's absenteeism, waste and quality.

questions.question_text: AAB must upskill 18 production staff on the new convection ovens before the central kitchen opens. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should AAB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on AAB's own convection ovens is directly relevant to the exact machines, bake programmes and quality standards used in the new kitchen, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive during the run-up to launch, protecting the 2.1-day branch delivery promise and daily output. Drawbacks are that trainers are production staff whose own work suffers, bad habits can be passed on informally, and the hygiene recertification element is harder to evidence for supermarket auditors without certificates.

Off-the-job training: The insert defines the technical college course as off-the-job hygiene certification at $700 per employee, and all 18 staff need it — that is $12,600 in total (18 × $700 = $12,600), affordable against the $620,000 investment and the $400,000 bank loan. The course certificates hygiene only; it does not cover convection-oven operation, which the insert assigns to on-the-job coaching, so machine-specific coaching would still be required. However, the course removes 18 of 38 staff from the line during training weeks, cutting short-term capacity and risking delivery failures just before launch.

Decision: AAB should choose on-the-job training for the six weeks before the kitchen opens, adding short college sessions for the two lead bakers. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further strain while absenteeism is at 8%, and loss of capacity would be unacceptable just before launch. Full off-the-job training is rejected as too disruptive and too generic for the pre-launch period; AAB can add college visits later once the line stabilises, and will still need the $700 per employee hygiene recertification for all 18 staff to satisfy auditors. Keeping training in-house through the launch also lets the two lead bakers coach the rest, freeing the technical college budget for the remaining certification outside peak production.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to AAB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of AAB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of AAB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AAB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $225,000 ÷ ($8.00 − $4.40) = $225,000 ÷ $3.60 = 62,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 62,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.00 − $4.40 = $3.60. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AAB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. AAB's managers can compare the 62,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units to confirm the bakery is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 37,500 units, informing whether the new central kitchen should commit to full capacity and the pre-order launch targets.
2. Contribution per unit of $3.60 lets managers model discounts negotiated with supermarket chains, for example trimming the price from $8.00 to $7.60 would drop contribution to $3.20, letting them judge whether the resulting volume gain would still cover the $225,000 fixed costs and the $400,000 bank loan repayments.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $225,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume targets used to check that the new kitchen can service the $400,000 ten-year bank loan and the $620,000 investment before committing further retained profit, and to time reorders of flour and butter against the 9.6% input-cost inflation.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($225,000 ÷ 100,000 units + $4.40 = $6.65 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, identify waste driving the 7% unsold-stock figure, and decide whether to renegotiate the $4.40 variable cost with suppliers or raise prices for the premium sourdough line.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 62,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.60 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained in detail: First, AAB's managers can compare the 62,500-unit break-even output with the current 100,000-unit run to confirm a margin of safety of 37,500 units, giving confidence that the central kitchen can also absorb pre-order growth before any pricing changes are agreed with supermarket chains. Second, the $3.60 contribution per unit lets managers model promotional discounts — a cut to $7.60 would leave only $3.20 per unit, so any volume offer must still cover the $225,000 fixed costs and the $400,000 ten-year bank loan repayments. Third, unit cost benchmarking ($225,000 ÷ 100,000 units + $4.40 = $6.65 a unit) gives AAB a quarterly yardstick for spotting waste, tracking the 7% unsold-stock figure and challenging flour and butter suppliers amid the 9.6% input-cost rise. Fourth, knowing fixed costs of $225,000 and contribution per unit supports loan feasibility checks before the remaining $220,000 retained profit is committed to the $620,000 kitchen, so the expansion does not outrun cash generation from the online pre-order platform.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AAB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has AAB's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios gives the stronger evidence, and why? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.82 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.18 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $175,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $75,000 + $55,000 = $200,000. CR 2024 = $175,000 ÷ $125,000 current liabilities = 1.40; CR 2025 = $200,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.82. AT 2024 = ($175,000 − $85,000) ÷ $125,000 = $90,000 ÷ $125,000 = 0.72; AT 2025 = ($200,000 − $70,000) ÷ $110,000 = $130,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.18.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. Current assets rose from $175,000 to $200,000 while current liabilities fell from $125,000 to $110,000, so short-term coverage improved on both measures. The AT line, which excludes inventories, rose from 0.72 to 1.18, meaning AAB no longer depends on selling perishable stock to pay its immediate debts — vital while it services a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and builds the $620,000 central kitchen. Cash nearly doubled from $30,000 to $55,000 and inventories were cut from $85,000 to $70,000, showing tighter stock rotation of fresh sourdough. Which ratio gives the stronger evidence? The acid test is the stronger indicator of AAB's short-term solvency because it excludes inventories — perishable fresh bread that may need discounting or write-off to realise cash — and it rose from 0.72 to 1.18, confirming that the stronger liquidity rests on cash and receivables rather than on stock build-up. Two concerns remain: trade receivables climbed from $60,000 to $75,000, tying up cash that could fund the kitchen, and the inventory reduction must not undershoot fresh-bread demand from the 46% of weekly sourdough buyers.

Conclusion: AAB's financial position has improved. Both the CR (1.40 to 1.82) and the AT (0.72 to 1.18) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is the $75,000 of trade receivables, so AAB should tighten credit control with its supermarket customers while proceeding with the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether AAB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AAB of switching its delivery vans to electric vehicles.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Electric vans would cut AAB's fuel and maintenance costs on the 2.1-day branch delivery routes, reinforcing the low-waste, low-emission story of the new central kitchen. Lower running costs would protect the $4.40 variable cost per unit and appeal to the 58% of surveyed shoppers willing to pre-order online and the 46% who buy sourdough weekly, many of whom reward visible sustainability, helping AAB win or keep supermarket listings alongside the $620,000 investment.

Disadvantage: Electric vans cost more to buy upfront and need charging points at the central kitchen and branches, straining cash while AAB already finances a $400,000 bank loan and a $220,000 retained profit commitment. If charging infrastructure is unreliable, the 2.1-day delivery promise to branches and supermarkets could slip, damaging AAB's reputation for freshness exactly when the online pre-order launch depends on dependable, chilled-quality delivery and when the 7% unsold-stock waste problem is already pressuring margins across the bakery.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AAB's delivery promise, research data and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in flour and butter input costs will affect AAB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If AAB's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% rise adds about $3,000 a year to financing costs and raises the effective burden on top of the $225,000 fixed costs. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious about premium bakery products, which could slow the 2.8% growth in premium bakery spending, and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $620,000 kitchen. The direct cost impact is modest, and AAB can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate or negotiating with its bank.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $12.74 per hour): The insert gives a 7.1% rise from $11.90 to $12.74 — a derived delta of $0.84 per hour ($12.74 − $11.90; check: 7.1% × $11.90 ≈ $0.84). Roles anchored to the floor become more expensive from April 2026, and pay bands above the floor typically shift as well. The insert does not state hours worked per worker, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, with 38 wage-dependent posts in a business producing 100,000 units a year, every hour worked becomes more expensive, so the annual impact would be material and democratic leadership and productivity gains (100,000 units ÷ 38 staff ≈ 2,632 units per worker) would need to offset it through lower absenteeism and waste.

Input cost inflation (9.6% flour and butter): The insert gives a $4.40 variable cost per unit and a 9.6% year-on-year rise in flour and butter input costs. Taking the entire variable cost as an upper bound: 9.6% × $4.40 = about $0.42 per unit; at 100,000 units a year that is roughly $42,000 a year (100,000 × $0.42, derivation shown; an upper bound since not all of the $4.40 is flour and butter). Even a fraction of that bound would directly erode the $3.60 contribution per unit and squeeze the margin that justifies the $620,000 expansion, though AAB can partially recover through the premium sourdough positioning and supermarket price talks, since consumer spending on premium bakery products still grew 2.8%.

Conclusion: The minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on AAB overall. The insert gives no cap on the hours affected, so a $0.84-an-hour rise applies mechanically to every working hour across the 38-strong workforce, directly threatening the $620,000 expansion business case, while the 9.6% input-cost rise is bounded at roughly $42,000 a year (an upper bound) against which premium positioning and supermarket price talks offer some cover, and the interest-rate rise is the smallest risk at about $3,000 a year and can be fixed or hedged. AAB should therefore plan its April 2026 pay bands and productivity drive carefully, while managing input inflation daily through pricing and protecting cash for the pre-order launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AAB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AAB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AAB with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
